title: Drought lowered bird counts in two US warm deserts in independent periods, but explained only one quarter to one half of the 1968-2025 decline; Sonoran-Mojave links came from spring heat
abstract: We tested the claim of van den Bosch et al. (2025) that increased drought drives bird declines in US warm deserts. That study used 47 Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) routes in 1998-2022 without observer effects. We used the full BBS 2026 release (1968-2025), a 12-month SPEI from NOAA nClimGrid, and Poisson models with route-observer and year fixed effects. The total count of the paper's 38 species decreased by 9.0% (95% interval 1.3 to 16.0) per drought unit on 49 Sonoran-Mojave routes (BCR 33) in 1998-2022. The link also occurred in an independent period (paper routes 1968-1997: -12.7%) and in an independent warm desert (Chihuahuan, BCR 35, 1968-2025: -6.4%). It was absent in the cold Great Basin (-1.2%, interval includes zero). The drought trend explained only 32% (15 to 56%) of the 21% per decade decrease in BCR 33 in 1998-2022, and 25% (12 to 47%) of the 1968-2025 decrease in BCR 35. Before 1998 the species did not decrease. In BCR 33 the link came from spring heat (-14% per 1 C) with no carry-over to the next year, and survey-morning temperature did not explain it. In BCR 35, precipitation and the previous summer monsoon carried the link. Species slopes were weak and not repeatable between periods. In the released paper data, observer effects reduced the linear decline from -13% to -6% per decade but did not change the drought coefficient. Limitations: counts are indices, so weather can change detection; our SPEI depends strongly on temperature; warm-desert samples are small; we did not test land cover or air pollution. Code, derived public-domain tables, results and figures are included.
